Modelling note. The physical inscribed surface and the text it bears are two things. CRMtex TX1 Written Text, a subclass of E25 Human-Made Feature, is the family's dedicated class for the marks themselves; the text those marks spell out is the instance of E34 Inscription, which the ding also carries directly. E34's own scope note insists on this split, and it is what lets Chen Jieqi's rubbings carry the same instance of E34 as the vessel does.

Statement. 500 characters arranged in 32 lines, the longest inscription among the ancient Chinese bronze inscriptions and "the longest such inscription known today". Content summary. The inscription text bears witness to the "King Xuan restoration" in Western Zhou history. The first part of the text consists of King Xuan's instructions to the Duke of Mao. The middle portion recounts how the King, upon taking the throne, fondly recalled how King Wen of Zhou and King Wu of Zhou had enjoyed the Mandate of Heaven and established the kingdom, as well as the King's vigilance and apprehension over inheriting the Mandate himself. The latter part lists in detail the generous gifts the King had bestowed upon the Duke of Mao. In closing, the Duke of Mao expresses his gratitude to the King, and presents the ding as an expression thereof for future generations. The article dates the object at two different grains and never reconciles them. The infobox gives "c. 805 BCE"; the running text says only that the vessel is "from the Western Zhou dynasty (c. 1045-771 BCE)" and "dates from the reign of King Xuan of Zhou". These are not presented as rival datings and the article cites no disagreement, so this is modelled as one time-span, carrying the narrowest claim (circa 805 BCE) with P82 at some time within and P79/P80 for the "circa", and nested inside the wider Western Zhou span with P86 falls within. The reign is attached to the production event itself with P10 falls within.
